title: Keep Only the Values That Appear Once
statement:
`head` is the head of a linked list whose values are **sorted** from smallest to largest. Remove **every node whose value appears more than once** in the list (not just the extra copies: all the copies go). Return the head of the resulting list, which keeps only the values that occur exactly once.

Re-link the existing nodes; do not build a new list.

examples.explanation: 2 and 4 each appear twice, so every copy of them is removed.
The only value repeats, so nothing is left.

hints.nudge: The first node may have to go too, so you need a node in front of the head. And when you find a run of equal values, you must remove the whole run, not all but one.
hints.pattern: A dummy node, a pointer `prev` to the last node that stays; at each step check whether the next node starts a run of equal values and, if so, skip the whole run.
hints.pseudocode:
dummy.next = head; prev = dummy; cur = head
while cur:
  if cur.next and cur.next.val == cur.val:
    v = cur.val; while cur and cur.val == v: cur = cur.next
    prev.next = cur
  else: prev = cur; cur = cur.next
return dummy.next
hints.walkthrough: Counting the values in a map and filtering needs extra memory and ignores that the list is sorted. Because it is sorted, equal values sit in a block. Walk with `cur`. If `cur` and the node after it have the same value, you are at the start of a run of duplicates: remember the value and move `cur` forward until the value changes, then link `prev` straight to the first node after the run. Otherwise `cur` is a value that appears once: it stays, so `prev` moves to it. The dummy node covers the case where the head itself is part of a run. O(n) time, O(1) extra memory.
